article.overview: A surface communications terminal is a radio station on the lunar surface that links surface assets, such as landers, rovers, astronauts and scientific instruments, to other assets or to Earth. It can communicate directly with ground stations on Earth or through lunar orbital relay satellites. Because the Moon's far side is not in direct line of sight from Earth, and because a surface experiment may need a local radio link before its data can reach an orbiter or ground station, the terminal is a key element of lunar communications infrastructure. There is no single standard design for this payload class. The examples reviewed here are a historical Apollo relay unit, a lander-mounted user terminal that had not flown in the sources reviewed, and NASA Glenn concept studies for a surface relay.
article.description: A surface communications terminal typically combines a radio transceiver, an antenna, a digital modem or software-defined radio, a power and thermal system, and a network or protocol interface. It is installed on a fixed station, a lander or a mobile platform. Its job is to receive data and voice from surface users, such as astronauts, rovers, instruments or other landers, and transmit them onward. Depending on the architecture, the onward link may go directly to Earth ground stations, or it may pass through a lunar orbital relay such as ESA's Lunar Pathfinder. The terminal therefore sits between short-range surface links and longer-range space links. Some designs also act as a base station for a local wireless network, allowing surface assets to use common network protocols rather than individual point-to-point radio links. This general description is an engineering summary; the specific configuration of each example is given below.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The primary purpose is to move data, voice and video between surface users and Earth or orbit. For science payloads, the terminal returns instrument data that would otherwise have to be stored onboard until a later pass. For crewed missions, it supports voice and video links during extravehicular activity. For robotic missions, it supports telemetry and commanding of landers and rovers. The 1970 RCA design description of the Apollo Lunar Communications Relay Unit (LCRU) identifies relay of voice, data and colour television as its function [5]. The JPL User Terminal is intended to test a low-cost lunar relay link and to help commission ESA's Lunar Pathfinder relay [3]. NASA Glenn's Lunar Surface Relay studies propose a base-station terminal for surface networks, providing voice, data and video services [1].
article.operating_principle: A surface terminal receives signals from surface assets on one radio link and forwards them on another. In a relay architecture, the surface link usually uses a channel suited to short range, while the onward link to an orbiter or Earth uses a band suited to the longer path. The JPL User Terminal implements a new S-band version of the Proximity-1 protocol, specified in 2024, for exchanging data with a relay satellite [3]. The NASA Glenn concept describes a terminal that could provide 3GPP-based and Wi-Fi network services to surface assets, so that users connect to the terminal as they would to a local network [1]. Antennas are central to the design: directional antennas improve link margin toward a relay or Earth, while wider-beam antennas serve local users. These are general engineering principles; the specific bands, power levels and antenna types of any given terminal must be taken from its own documentation.
article.scientific_importance: Surface communications determine how much scientific and operational value a lunar mission can return. Without a reliable link, surface instruments must store data until a relay or direct Earth pass is available, and crews on the surface lose real-time voice contact with mission control. The Apollo program demonstrated this need directly: the Lunar Communications Relay Unit (LCRU) was designed to relay voice, data and colour television from lunar surface locations far beyond the lunar module landing site [5]. Later concepts extend the same principle to networks of surface assets, in which a terminal acts as a base station for several users and routes their traffic to Earth [1]. The scientific importance of such links is largely indirect, but significant, because they increase the usefulness of other payloads.

physical_specifications.note: There is no single universal mass, size or power figure for a surface communications terminal. The values below apply only to the named example. Where a figure was not verified in the sources reviewed, it is marked as not publicly specified rather than estimated.

examples.name: Apollo Lunar Communications Relay Unit (LCRU)
examples.type: Historical lunar surface relay equipment from the Apollo programme
examples.flight_status: Used on Apollo 16 per the Apollo 16 Lunar Surface Journal record, which shows the LCRU removed from the lunar roving vehicle's stowage assembly during traverse preparation. The Smithsonian record associates rover use with Apollo 15, 16 and 17. The museum unit (RCA-manufactured, inventory A19761822000) is recorded as unflown and is not evidence about flight equipment performance.
examples.function: Portable communications package that relays voice, data and colour television from lunar surface locations far beyond the lunar module landing site to Earth, and relays ground voice to the extravehicular crew (1970 RCA system design description).
examples.radio_bands: Not verified. Specific S-band and VHF parameters reported in an OCR-degraded excerpt of a 1971 crew training manual were not checked against the original and are omitted.
examples.storage_pallet_note: The Smithsonian record gives 123.2 x 122.6 x 86.4 cm and 117.9 kg for a storage pallet holding this unit with two other objects. These figures describe the packaged arrangement and are not the mass or size of the relay unit alone.

examples.name: JPL User Terminal (Firefly Blue Ghost Mission 2)
examples.flight_status: Not flown in the sources reviewed. NASA's CLPS event page lists Firefly's Blue Ghost Mission 2 for 2027 and describes delivery to the lunar far side. JPL's August 2025 image release described the mission as slated for 2026. The sources conflict and no confirmed launch date was found.
examples.function: Low-cost lunar communications system. The lander's unit is planned to commission ESA's Lunar Pathfinder relay by exchanging test data with it. A second unit on the LuSEE-Night radio telescope is planned to send its data through Pathfinder after about 14 Earth days, when the lander stops operating. The terminal can also communicate with Firefly's Elytra Dark orbiter.
examples.radio_bands: A new S-band version of the Proximity-1 protocol, specified in 2024.

examples.name: NASA Glenn Lunar Surface Relay concepts (stationary and mobile surface terminals)
examples.flight_status: No flight hardware reported. Designs and trade studies only.
examples.function: Base-station terminal for surface assets providing 3GPP and Wi-Fi network services for voice, data and video. Four wireless surface terminal designs (one stationary, three mobile) were developed to compare mass, power and cost drivers and trade-offs. Terminals are powered by either a radioisotope/battery system or a solar-array/battery system, and transmit to Earth through lunar orbital relays or directly.
examples.mobile_concept: An associated NASA Glenn paper is titled as a concept to provide relay links to surface assets. Its requirement values, data rates and bands could not be extracted in this pass.
examples.radio_bands: Not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions depend heavily on the architecture. The Apollo relay was a portable package carried on the lunar roving vehicle. The museum storage pallet that holds one Communications Relay Unit with two other objects measures 123.2 x 122.6 x 86.4 cm, a figure that does not describe the unit alone. The JPL User Terminal's dimensions are not stated in the sources reviewed. The NASA Glenn surface terminal concepts were compared for mass and power, but their dimensions were not extracted.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass was not verified for any example in this article. The Smithsonian record gives 117.9 kg for the storage pallet arrangement holding three objects, which is not the relay unit's mass. Mass determines lander capacity and launch requirements, so it is the most important value to confirm from primary documentation before any design comparison.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power requirements are not publicly specified for the examples in this article. The NASA Glenn concepts assess radioisotope/battery and solar-array/battery options for their terminals. The JPL User Terminal's power source is not stated in the sources reviewed, and no verified wattage is given for the Apollo relay.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A surface terminal must operate through the lunar day–night cycle. The lunar night lasts roughly 14 Earth days, which constrains solar-powered designs and is one reason the Lunar Surface Relay study compared radioisotope/battery and solar-array/battery power variants [1]. Terminals also face vacuum, wide temperature swings, dust and radiation, and they must keep their antennas pointed toward a relay or Earth. A stable installation matters because support-structure movement can disturb antenna pointing. These are general engineering considerations rather than requirements taken from a verified specification. The environmental qualification of the examples above is not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.
article.limitations: A terminal is useful only when a link exists at the right time. Surface-to-relay links depend on line of sight, antenna pointing and orbital geometry, so a single terminal cannot provide continuous Earth contact. Most surface terminal work in the reviewed sources is still at the design or demonstration stage. The JPL User Terminal's data-relay role depends on the availability of the relay satellite, and the Lunar Surface Relay studies have not been shown to be built [1][2]. The Apollo LCRU was a voice and television relay for crew operations, so its design priorities differ from those of a modern data-focused terminal.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A surface communications terminal is delivered either as a lander-mounted payload or as a crew-carried package. The transport chain is similar in both cases: integration with a spacecraft on Earth, launch, transfer to the Moon, landing, deployment, setup, and connection to power and data.
transportation_process: Integrate the terminal, antenna and electronics with the lander or rover on Earth, including thermal and mechanical interfaces.
Launch on a launch vehicle and transfer toward the Moon.
Land the terminal on the surface with its host vehicle.
Deploy and orient the antenna toward the relay or Earth.
Connect power, data and thermal control, then commission the link.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The Apollo relay was carried on the lunar roving vehicle and removed from its stowage assembly by the crew during traverse preparation [6]. The JPL User Terminal is described as lander-associated, with its lander unit planned to commission Lunar Pathfinder [3]; its deployment mechanism is not described in the sources reviewed. The Lunar Surface Relay concepts include stationary and mobile variants, and their deployment methods were not extracted in this pass [1][2].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo 16 provides a crewed example, in which the LCRU was removed from the rover's stowage during traverse preparation [6]. The 1970 design paper describes the unit as a portable package [5]. If it flies, the JPL User Terminal on Blue Ghost Mission 2 would be a robotic example of a lander-mounted relay test [3][4].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: JPL lists the User Terminal as a payload of Firefly's Blue Ghost Mission 2 lander [3][4]. That is manifest evidence, not a verified mechanical or electrical interface specification. The Apollo LCRU's transport on the rover is supported by the historical record [6]. No Lunar Surface Relay concept has been verified for a named lander or rover, and this article does not assert compatibility for any of them.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo relay was designed to extend lunar surface communications from sites far beyond the landing site, so that crews could keep voice and television links while working away from the lander [5][6]. The Smithsonian holds an unflown counterpart of the relay unit [7]. The JPL User Terminal represents a newer, lower-cost approach to a lunar relay link [3], and NASA Glenn's Lunar Surface Relay studies explore networked surface terminals for future missions [1][2].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The name "surface communications terminal" describes a function rather than one hardware design, so the examples above are not interchangeable. The Apollo LCRU is historical, and the Lunar Surface Journal records it being carried on the Apollo 16 lunar roving vehicle [6], but the mass, dimensions, power and radio figures for the flight equipment could not be verified in this research pass. The JPL User Terminal had not flown in the sources reviewed, and sources disagree on its launch timing. The Lunar Surface Relay studies are design and trade studies whose full-text requirement values could not be extracted in this pass, so no performance figures are reported for them. This article is not a certified design specification for a new terminal.
evidence_gaps: Mass, dimensions, power and radio parameters of the flown Apollo LCRU are not verified. An OCR-degraded 1971 crew training manual excerpt reports per-unit figures that could not be checked against the original.
The full text of the ICSSC 2023 Lunar Surface Relay paper and the ASCEND LSR-M paper could not be extracted in this run, so their mass, power, data-rate and band values are not reproduced.
The JPL User Terminal launch date conflicts across sources: 2026 in JPL's August 2025 release and 2027 on NASA's CLPS event page. No confirmed launch was found.
ESA Lunar Pathfinder schedule and specifications could not be verified from a citable page.
The Smithsonian collection-media item's direct image asset was not verified, and its image content was not reviewed.
Lander-specific interface evidence beyond JPL's payload listing for Blue Ghost Mission 2 was not found.

data_quality_notes: Catalogue confirmed: ID 191, 'Surface communications terminal', category 9 'Navigation, communication and geodesy'.

The ICSSC 2023 Lunar Surface Relay paper PDF and the ASCEND LSR-M paper PDF returned binary data that could not be text-extracted in this run. Their mass, power, data-rate and band values are therefore not reproduced; mentions of these studies rely on abstract and title text only.

The Apollo 16 LCRU stowage detail and the Apollo rover mission context were taken from search-result excerpts of the Lunar Surface Journal and Air and Space Museum pages, not from a full read of those pages.

An OCR-degraded search excerpt of a 1971 LCRU crew training manual (LRTM-SY-1) reported per-unit dimensions, weights and VHF figures. These could not be verified against the original and are excluded from the specification fields.
The Smithsonian object record describes the museum unit as unflown. This does not describe the flight equipment.

Launch timing for Firefly Blue Ghost Mission 2 conflicts: JPL's August 2025 release says 2026, NASA's CLPS event page says 2027, and third-party trackers vary. No launch was confirmed as of the research date.
The ESA Lunar Pathfinder page (bsgn.esa.int) was read but not cited. Its only usable URL carries a query string, and removing it would point to a different homepage.
The mobile Lunar Surface Relay requirement values (coverage distance, bands, lifetime) reported in a search summary were not confirmed from the full paper and are not included.
The JPL image asset was checked visually and matches the caption's description of an engineer working on the User Terminal hardware. The Smithsonian collection-media item was not fetched or reviewed.
